Metabolic proﬁling reveals that salidroside antagonizes hypoxic injury via
modulating energy and lipid metabolism in cardiomyocytes
Wenting Liaoa, Jia Liue, Shiming Wanga, Zhen Xuea, Feng Zhenga, Feng Fengb,d, Wenyuan Liua,c,*
a Department of Pharmaceutical Analysis, China Pharmaceutical University, Nanjing 210009, China
b The Joint Laboratory of Chinese Pharmaceutical University and Taian City Central Hospital, Taian City Central Hospital, Taian 271000, China
c Hangzhou Institute of Pharmaceutical Innovation, China Pharmaceutical University, 291 Fucheng Lu, Hangzhou 310018, China
d Jiangsu Food and Pharmaceutical Science College, Huaian 223003, China
e Pharmic Laboratory Animal Center, China Pharmaceutical University, Nanjing 210009, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Metabolomics
UPLC-QTOFMS
Salidroside
Hypoxic injury
Drug targets
A B S T R A C T
Hypoxia induces cardiomyocytes injury, which further triggers the occurrence and development of cardiovas-
cular diseases. There is a paucity of speciﬁc treatment options available with proven eﬃcacy. Chinese patented
pharmaceutical product Salidroside (Sal) has potent eﬃcacy on treating hypoxic injury. However, the molecular
mechanism remains obscure. In the present study, a UPLC-QTOFMS-based metabolomic method combined with
cell viability and apoptosis assays were established to explore the therapeutic mechanisms of Sal against hypoxic
injury. Signiﬁcant protective eﬀects of Sal against inhibited cell viability and apoptosis induced by hypoxic
injury were observed in the pharmacodynamic evaluation. Moreover, 40 signiﬁcantly changed metabolites re-
lated to hypoxic injury were identiﬁed, of which, 26 can be signiﬁcantly regulated by Sal. Metabolic pathway
enrichment analysis revealed that the mechanisms of Sal against hypoxic injury may be attributed to modulating
the disordered homeostasis of energy and lipid metabolism. The present study provides new experimental in-
formation on the pathogenesis of hypoxia, unravels the potential targeted metabolic pathways of Sal against
hypoxia on the whole metabolic network and highlights the importance of metabolomics as a potential tool for
deciphering drug-targeted metabolic pathways.
1. Introduction
Hypoxia is a pervasive pathophysiological process under various
cellular conditions, such as high altitude, ageing, inﬂammation, cardi-
ovascular and respiratory failures, wounds and even cancer. Many or-
gans need oxygen for their survival, and cardiovascular and respiratory
systems
acquire
and
distribute
oxygen
to
the
various
tissues.
Myocardial hypoxia in long-term usually cause a series of serious
clinical diseases, such as atherosclerosis, hypertension and myocardial
ischemia. Hypoxic myocardial injury has increasingly attracted the at-
tention of clinicians. Although several pharmacological strategies have
been developed to reduce the injury, there is still lack of eﬀective
therapeutic approaches due to its complicated molecular mechanisms
[1]. H9c2 cardiomyocytes, directly derived from corresponding tissue,
are a simple and controllable system that characterizes the local me-
tabolic alterations of related organs and can be employed to reﬂect the
exact protective mechanisms of drugs on cell damage.
Salidroside (Sal), an acknowledged bioactive ingredient from
Rhodiola rosea, has been documented to exhibit various pharmacolo-
gical activities such as anti-oxidation, anti-inﬂammation, anti-cancer,
anti-fatigue, and anti-virus [2–5]. In China, Sal is widely used for the
clinical prevention and treatment of acute mountain sickness and
cardio-cerebrovascular diseases. Further studies have found that Sal
could antagonize ischemic hypoxic cytotoxic eﬀects by participating in
several signaling pathways, including regulating HIF-1α, PI3K, MAPK,
NF-κB signaling pathway [6–9], repressing caspase-dependent apop-
tosis, increasing EPO [9], VEGF [10], BcL-2 expression [3,11], and
restoring the function of sodium and potassium channels [12]. How-
ever, the comprehensive protective mechanisms of Sal in mimic high
aititude hypoxia remain obscure.
A cell metabolic proﬁle is crucial for a holistic understanding of cell
properties and function, and also critical for the development of drugs
and markers for special cellular phenotypes. Cell metabolomics, a re-
ﬂection of the cell phenotype, had been proved to be an eﬀective ap-
proach to screen the perturbed metabolic pathways related to disease
processes
and
drug-targeted
metabolic
pathways

perspective [13]. In this study, a model of hypoxic injury in H9c2
cardiomyocytes was employed to resemble the high-altitude hypoxic
injury in vivo. Furthermore, cell viability and apoptosis assays were
applied to explore the cardiac protective eﬀects of Sal against hypoxic
myocardial injury in cultured cardiomyocytes, and cell metabolomics
based on an UPLC-QTOFMS technique was developed to investigate the
metabolome perturbations in hypoxic H9c2 cells and the protective
eﬀects of Sal. This study may provide a valuable insight into the un-
derstanding of pathological changes of hypoxic injury and intervention
mechanism of Sal.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Chemicals and reagents
Salidroside (purity > 99 %) was purchased from the National
Institute for the Control of Pharmaceutical and Biological Products
(Beijing, China) and its chemical structure was presented in Fig.1.
HPLC-grade methanol and acetonitrile (ACN) were purchased from
Merck (Darmstadt, Germany). Formic acid was obtained from Fluka
(Buchs,
Switzerland).
Lysophosphatidylcholine(18:0),
lysopho-
sphatidylethanolamine
(16:0),
lysophosphatidylethanolamine(18:0),
sphingosine, sphinganine, phytosphingosine, palmitoylcarnitine, and
searoylcarnitine were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO).
Succinic acid, malic acid, citric acid, histidine, glutamine, aspartic acid,
tyrosine,
leucine,
tryptophan and
carnitine were obtained from
Shanghai Jingchun Reagent Co., LTD.
2.2. Cell culture
The rat embryonic cardiac cells (H9c2, ATCC) were cultured in
DMEM (Invitrogen) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS,
Hyclone) at 37 °C with 5 % CO2. When cell conﬂuency reached 70 %–80
%, H9c2 cells were used for experiments. For all the treatment groups,
H9c2 cells were preincubated with Sal for 2 h before initiating hypoxia.
Where indicated, hypoxia (1 % O2) was achieved by a mixture of ultra-
high purity gases (1 % O2, 5 % CO2, 94 % N2) in a 37 °C incubator
(Thermo Fisher).
2.3. Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK8) assay
H9c2 cells (5 × 104 cells/mL) were cultured in 96-well plates
overnight, followed by pretreating with diﬀerent concentrations of Sal
(10–100 μM) for 2 h and exposure to hypoxia for another 24 h, 48 h or
72 h. The CCK8 assay was performed following the manufacturer’s
protocol. The optical density (OD) value was detected at 450 nm using a
Universal Microplate Reader (Bio-Tek Instruments, Inc.).
2.4. Cell apoptosis assays
For detection of apoptosis cells, H9c2 cells (5 × 104 cells/mL) were
cultured in 6-well plates overnight, followed by pretreating with 25 μM
Sal for 2 h and exposure to hypoxia for another 24 h or 48 h. The
concentration of Sal and the time for incubation were based on the
abovementioned CCK8 assay. After hypoxia, H9c2 cells were detached,
washed and incubated in 200 μL binding buﬀer, 2 μL annexin V-FITC
and 2 μL of propidium iodide (PI) (Invitrogen, Shanghai, China) at room
temperature for 15 min in the dark. Then, 300 μL binding buﬀer was
added, and cells were then analyzed in a FACSCalibur ﬂow cytometer
(Becton- Dickinson, USA). Annexin V positive cells were labeled as
apoptotic cells, and Annexin V negative but PI positive cells were
marked as necrotic cells. PI percentage was utilized as cell death per-
centage.
2.5. Cell quenching
For metabolite measurements, H9c2 cells were cultured in a 10 cm
dish overnight, and then pretreated with 25 μM Sal for 2 h. After 24 h or
48 h of hypoxia, the culture medium was removed from the culture
dish, cells was quickly washed twice with ice-cold phosphate-buﬀered
saline (PBS, pH 7.4). The residual PBS was removed by vacuum. Cells
were then quenched using 1.5 mL 80 % HPLC-grade methanol (−40 °C)
[14]. Next, cells were gently detached from the culture dish using a cell
lifter. The methanol solution containing the quenched cells was pi-
petted into a 2 mL centrifuge tube and frozen in liquid nitrogen until
extraction. In addition, three parallel dishes of cells were trypsinized
and counted using a hemocytometer (Neubauer chamber), subsequent
metabolite measurements were normalized to cell count.
2.6. Samples preparation
The extraction of intracellular metabolites from H9c2 cells was
performed as previously described with minor modiﬁcations [14].
Brieﬂy, quenched cells were thawed in an ice bath for 10 min, spiked
with the internal standard (5 μL of 1 mg/mL L-2-chlorophenylalanine),
and then lysed by the application of two freeze-thaw cycles (freezing in
liquid nitrogen for 10 min, thawing in an ice bath for 10 min). After
that, the samples were ultrasonicated in an ice bath ultrasonicator for
15 min and subsequently centrifuged at 18,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The
extract was dried using a Speed Vac (SPD111 V Savant, Thermo Fisher
Scientiﬁc) and then reconstituted in 150 μL 70 % acetonitrile, vortexed
brieﬂy, and centrifuged at 18,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C to remove any
insoluble components. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by
pooling and mixing the same volume of each sample and then were
analyzed ﬁve times at the beginning of the run and injected once after
every 8 injections of the random sequenced samples.
2.7. UPLC-QTOFMS analysis
UPLC-QTOFMS analysis was performed on a Agilent 1290 Inﬁnity
LC system coupled to an Agilent 6530 Accurate-Mass Quadrupole Time-
of-Flight (Q-TOF) mass spectrometer (Agilent, USA). An acquity UPLC
BEH C18 column (2.1 mm × 100 mm, 1.7 μm, Waters, Milford, MA) was
used for for sample separation at 40 °C. The mobile phase consisted of
0.1 % formic acid (A) and ACN modiﬁed with 0.1 % formic acid (B),
with gradient elution of 5 % B at 0–2 min, 5 %–95 % B at 2–17 min, 95
% B at 17–19 min. The total run time was 24 min including equilibra-
tion. The ﬂow rate was 400 μL/min and the injection volume was 3 μL.
An electrospray ionization (ESI) source interface was used, and was
set in both positive and negative modes so as to monitor as many ions as
possible. The mass spectrometric conditions were optimized as follows:
capillary voltage, 3.5 kV; drying gas, 11 L/min; gas temperature,
350 °C; nebulizer pressure, 45 psig; fragmentor voltage, 120 V; and
skimmer voltage, 60 V. Data were collected in a centroid mode and the
mass range was set at m/z 50−1000. Potential biomarkers were ana-
lysed by MS/MS. MS spectra were collected at 2 spectra/s, and MS/MS
spectra were collected at 0.5 spectra/s, with a medium isolation
window (∼4 m/z) and a ﬁxed collision energy of 20 V. The same MS
parameters was set in negative mode as that in positive mode.

2.8. Metabolic proﬁling and pathway analysis
The raw data from the nontargeted analysis acquired by UPLC-
QTOFMS were converted to mzData formats via Agilent MassHunter
Qualitative software. The program XCMS (http://metlin.scripps.edu/
download/) was applied for data pretreatment procedures such as
nonlinear retention time alignment, peak discrimination, ﬁltering,
alignment, matching, and identiﬁcation. The “80 % rule” was applied to
remove the missing value for each sample group [15]. The data matrix
(m/z, retention time, peak area) were exported to SIMCA-P Ver 14.1
(Umetrics, Sweden) for principal component analysis (PCA) and partial
least-squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA). The parameters R2Y
(cum) and Q2 (cum) reﬂected the goodness of ﬁtness and the predictive
ability of the models, respectively. The 7-fold cross-validation and 200-
times permutation test in SIMCA-P software was used to guard against
overﬁtting. Variable importance in the projection (VIP) analysis was
applied to obtain the signiﬁcant variables for subsequent metabolic
pathway analysis.
Metabolite identiﬁcation was performed according to our previous
work with minor modiﬁcation [16]. Brieﬂy, the quasi-molecular ions of
potential biomarkers were judged based on the positive and negative
ESI-Q-TOFMS scans. The chemical structures of the preliminarily
identiﬁed metabolites were obtained by searching the open-access da-
tabases of METLIN (http://metlin.scripps.edu) and HMDB (http://
www.hmdb.ca/) utilizing detected molecular
weights. Then, the
quasi-molecular ions were subjected to MS/MS analysis to narrow the
scope of target metabolites. Finally, these metabolites were further
conﬁrmed by available reference standards in our lab or the fragment
models in METLIN and HMDB databases.
Metabolic pathway analysis was performed with KEGG (http://
www.genome.jp/kegg/), MetaboAnalyst (http://www.metaboanalyst.
ca/MetaboAnalyst/), METLIN and HMDB.
2.9. Statistical analysis
The data were described as the means ± S.D. The diﬀerences of
groups were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s
multiple comparison. P < 0.05 was performed as a statistical diﬀer-
ence.
3. Results
3.1. Sal reduces hypoxia-induced cytotoxicity of H9c2 cells
H9c2 cells were pretreated with the diﬀerent concentrations of Sal
(10, 25, 50 or 100 μM) for 2 h, followed by hypoxia for 24, 48 or 72 h.
CCK8 results demonstrated that hypoxia signiﬁcantly inhibited H9c2
cell viability, which was alleviated by diﬀerent concentrations of Sal
except the 10 μM (Fig. 2). The cytoprotective eﬀect of Sal was dose-
dependent at 24 h, while no signiﬁcant diﬀerence was observed at the
other doses and time points. At 48 h, 25 μM Sal dramatically inhibited
hypoxia-induced H9c2 cell viability and showed the similar cytopro-
tective eﬀect with the other high-dose Sal. Therefore, 25 μM Sal pre-
treatment, followed by hypoxia for 24 h or 48 h was used as the optimal
concentration and time points in the subsequent experiments.
For cell apoptosis assays, H9c2 cells were pretreated with 25 μM for
2 h, followed by hypoxia for 24 or 48 h. As shown in Fig. 3, hypoxia
signiﬁcantly increased cell apoptosis, which was obviously decreased
by Sal at 48 h (P < 0.05), while no signiﬁcant diﬀerence between
groups was observed at 24 h (data not shown).
3.2. Metabolic proﬁling by UPLC-QTOFMS
The typical total ion current (TIC) chromatograms of UPLC-
QTOFMS are shown in Fig. S1. The stability of the analytical system
was evaluated by measuring the coeﬃcient of variation (CV) distribu-
tion across the QC samples. After normalization, the CV values of over
80 % ion features were below 30 %, which indicated that the present
analytical system had good repeatability. Totally, 708 and 732 ion
peaks were obtained from positive and negative ion modes of UPLC-
QTOFMS, respectively.
3.3. Multivariate statistical analysis and identiﬁcation of potential target
metabolites
After data normalization, an unsupervised PCA was initially con-
ducted to provide an overview of the variations among control, hy-
poxia, and Sal groups, and a separated trend of inter-group were ob-
served on the scores plot. Then, PLS-DA was employed to search ions
discriminating between control and hypoxia groups. Compared to the
unsupervised PCA model, the supervised PLS-DA was more focused on
the actual class discriminating variation. PLS-DA scores plot showed a
good discrimination between control and hypoxia groups (Fig. 4A–D).
The predictive ability of the model was assessed by internal validation
(R2Y and Q2), suggesting that the model possessed a satisfactory ﬁt with
high predictive power (Fig. 4A–D). The PLS-DA model was validated by
a random permutation test (200 times). According to the permutation
test, R2cum and Q2cum values were lower than the original values in
the validation plot, indicating that it was non-overﬁtting and reliable.
To investigate the eﬀects of Sal on hypoxia, LCeMS data sets were
further analyzed by PLS-DA. The PLS-DA scores plot showed that the
Sal group was located between the control and hypoxia groups,
showing a trend of recovering to the control group (Fig. 4E-H).
Metabolites of interest that signiﬁcantly contributed to the separa-
tion of the hypoxia and control groups were identiﬁed based on a
threshold of VIP values (VIP > 1.0) generated from PLS-DA model. To
select the potential biomarkers, these discriminated metabolites were
further restricted using one-way ANOVA (p < 0.05). According to the

above criterion, 40 signiﬁcantly altered metabolites were identiﬁed as
hypoxia-related biomarkers (Table 1). The heat map was used to vi-
sualize their relative levels of targeted metabolites in each individual
(Fig. 5). Compared to the model individuals, the relative concentration
of most targeted metabolites in the Sal-treated cells could be reversed
after pretreatment of Sal. The results of ANOVA showed that the re-
lative proﬁles of 26 cell metabolites was signiﬁcantly reversed by Sal
pretreatment (Table 1 and Fig. 6). Thus, Sal might regulate the multiple
metabolites to exhibit preventive eﬃcacy against hypxia.
3.4. Metabolic pathway analysis
To identify the potential hypoxia-induced and Sal-targeted meta-
bolic pathways, 40 signiﬁcantly perturbed metabolites in hypxia group
(versus control group) and 26 signiﬁcantly reversed metabolites in Sal-
treated
group
(versus
hypoxia
group)
were
imported
into
MetaboAnalyst 3.0. According to a threshold of the impact-value
(≥0.1), twelve metabolic pathways were identiﬁed as potential targets
for Sal, including phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis,
glutathione metabolism, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism,
valine, leucine and isoleucine biosynthesis, glyoxylate and dicarbox-
ylate metabolism, histidine metabolism, ether lipid metabolism, gly-
cerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism, tryptophan
metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, and citrate cycle (Fig. 7A and C). Of
the 12 hypoxia-induced metabolic pathways, glyoxylate and dicarbox-
ylate metabolism, ether lipid metabolism, glycerophospholipid meta-
bolism, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, and citrate cycle
involved in early hypoxia (Fig. S2 and Table S1), the remaning involved
in metabolic disorder in late hypoxia (Fig. S3 and Table S1). Sal-tar-
geted metabolic pathways were also identiﬁed, which were glutathione
metabolism, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, ether lipid me-
tabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism,
alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, and citrate cycle (Fig. 7B
and D). Of the 26 signiﬁcantly reversed metabolites identiﬁed from Sal-
targeted metabolic pathways, LysoPC(O-18:0) and LysoPE(O-18:1)
contributed to explaining ether lipid metabolism, LysoPE (LysoPE
(16:0), LysoPE(18:0), and LysoPE(P-16:0)), LysoPC(18:0), glyceropho-
sphocholine, and PC(18:4/P-18:1) were found and contributed to ex-
plaining glycerophospholipid metabolism. By relating these major me-
tabolic pathways, the schematic metabolic network of hypoxia-induced
and Sal modulation based on the KEGG database was constructed in
Fig.8.
4. Discussion
Sal has been proven to be distinguished in anti-hypoxia. However,
the underlying protective mechanisms of Sal against hypoxic myo-
cardial injury remain obscure. By identifying pathological metabolic
changes, metabolomics can point to potential new sites for therapeutic
intervention. In this study, an UPLC-QTOF/MS-based metabolomics
approach, combined with CCK8 test and apoptosis assay, was per-
formed to explore the potential mechanisms of Sal against hypoxia. The
increased H9c2 cells viability and decreased apoptosis rate in Sal group
provided evidence for the therapeutic eﬀect of Sal against hypoxia.

Moreover, a total of 40 metabolites related to hypoxia were identiﬁed,
of which, 26 metabolites were signiﬁcantly reversed after Sal pre-
treatment. The relevant metabolic pathways of these reversed meta-
bolites were constructed and seven metabolic pathways were ﬁltered
out to be the most important Sal-targeted metabolic pathways, which
were glutathione metabolism, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabo-
lism, ether lipid metabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphin-
golipid metabolism, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, and
citrate cycle. The major metabolic pathways are discussed below.
4.1. Energy metabolism
The citrate cycle is central to aerobic metabolism. Changes in three
pivotal intermediates including citric acid, succinic acid and malic acid
were observed in hypoxia group, indicating that the citrate cycle was
perturbed under hypoxic condition. An unbalanced citrate cycle was
indicative of decreased oxidative metabolism. Since the heart has per-
petually high energy demands, thus the diminished citrate cycle caused
by hypoxia may ultimately induce metabolic stress in cardiac tissue [3].
Whereas, when Sal was pretreated, the levels of citric acid, succinic acid
and malic acid were signiﬁcantly reversed.
As a carrier of long-chain fatty acids for β-oxidation or as a reservoir
pool of acyl-CoA, the carnitine system is essential for cell energy me-
tabolism [17]. The levels of long-chain acylcarnitines (LCAC) including
palmitoylcarnitine and stearoylcarnitine were signiﬁcantly increased,
and the levels of short-chain acylcarnitines (SCAC) including acetyl-L-
carnitine and propionyl-L-carnitine were signiﬁcantly decreased in hy-
poxia group compared to control group, suggesting that fatty acid
oxidation is inhibited under hypoxic condition. This ﬁnging is in con-
sistent with our previous report [16]. Other researchers have reported
that acute hypoxia caused the accumulation of LCAC [18], which
caused deleterious eﬀects in cardiac tissue and decreased cardiac
function [19], and may contribute to myocardial cell injury. In addition
to LCAC, propionylcarnitine and acetylcarnitine, two SCAC, were also
increased in hypoxia group, and the exact mechanism remains unclear.
Propionylcarnitine has been used in clinical treatment of cardiovascular
diseases [20]. It can be inferred that hypoxia can cause compensatory
increase of SCAC, which attenuate the damage of hypoxia by promoting

Increased nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), NADH and
decreased NAD+/NADH ratio were observed in hypoxia group (Fig.
S4), indicating that NAD+ metabolism and redox status were disturbed
during hypoxia exposure, which is supported by the result of decreased
glutathione (GSH), oxidized glutathione (GSSG), and GSH/GSSG ratio
(Fig. S4) in hypoxia group. NAD+ is a biological hydride acceptor that
forms the reduced dinucleotide NADH. The level of NAD+is linked to
many diseases by heavily impacting on metabolism, cellular viability,
and signaling pathways [21]. The NAD+/NADH couple is crucial for
driving a wide range of redox reactions in cellular bioenergetics [22].
Additionally, NAD+ is the precursor for the phosphorylated dinucleo-
tides NADP+ and NADPH, which play a key role in protecting cells from
reactive oxygen species (ROS) and in several cellular biosynthetic
pathways. Whereas, when cells were pretreated with Sal, the levels of
GSH, GSH/GSSG ratio, NADH, and NAD+/NADH were signiﬁcantly
reversed, which is line with the report indicating that salidroside
showed antioxidation eﬀect via modulating oxidative status [23].
These results imply that the protective mechanism of Sal against
hypoxic myocardial injury might be related to regulating the myo-
cardial energy metabolism and redox status by upregulating NAD+/
NADH and GSH/GSSG ratio.
4.2. Ether lipid metabolism and glycerophospholipid metabolism
Increased glycerophosphocholine (GPC), LysoPCs, LysoPEs, and
decreased PCs were observed in hypoxia group, which indicated that
ether lipid metabolism and glycerophospholipid metabolism was dis-
turbed during hypoxia exposure. Glycerophospholipids are essential
components of the membrane lipid bilayer. Cell membrane disruption is
closely related with membrane lipid metabolic abnormalities [24].
LysoPCs are produced by the hydrolysis of PC by phospholipase A2
(PLA2) which has been proved to be activated during hypoxia [25,26].
Furthermore, LysoPCs can be broken down to GPC by enzymolysis of
lyso-phospholipase. GPC, a speciﬁc indicator of phosphatidylcholine
breakdown, released only when cellular membrane function go astray

4.3. Sphingolipid metabolism
Sphingolipids play an important role in the structure of myocardial
cell membranes. The perturbed sphingolipid metabolism is regarded as
a pivotal event in the dysfunction of myocardial cells. The increased
levels of sphingosine, sphinganine, phytosphingosine, Cer(d18:0/14:0),
and Cer(d18:0/16:0) were observed in hypoxia group compared to
control group, indicating that sphingolipid metabolism was disturbed in
hypoxia injury. This ﬁnding is consistent with previous reports [28–30].
Understandably, these alterations may ascribe to the activation of some
key enzymes associated with sphingolipid metabolism. Serine palmi-
toyltransferas (SPT) is the rate-limiting enzyme of de-novo synthesis of
ceramide. Sphingomyelinases hydrolyse sphingomyelin, releasing cer-
amide and creating a cascade of bioactive lipids such as sphingosine
and sphinganine which were increased in hypoxia group. It was re-
ported that SPT and acid sphingomyelinase were found to be upregu-
lated under hypoxia conditions [6,29,31]. Whereas, when cells were
pretreated with Sal, the levels of sphingosine, sphinganine, Cer(d18:0/
14:0), and Cer(d18:0/16:0) were signiﬁcantly reversed. These results
implied that sphingolipid metabolism and related enzymes could be
considered as potential targets for drug development in the treatment of
myocardial injury caused by hypoxia.
5. Conclusion
In summary, UPLC-QTOFMS-based untargeted metabolomics ap-
proach coupled with CCK8 test and apoptosis assay was ﬁrstly applied
to explore the cytoprotective eﬀect of Sal against hypoxia, which dis-
closed glutathione metabolism, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabo-
lism, ether lipid metabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphin-
golipid metabolism, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, and
citrate cycle as the major targets underlying the protective eﬀect by Sal.
It demonstrated that metabolomics was a potential tool to discover the
metabolic biomarkers and identify drug targets. To obtain a more
complete understanding of Sal, future studies may focus on determining
the relationship between Sal and the targeted metabolic pathways
identiﬁed from this study.
